---
title: "CPU Scheduling — Waiting Time, Turnaround and Fairness"
description: "A rigorous introductory lesson with one small example, mathematical notation and a proof-oriented explanation."
---

## Start with an ordinary situation

Three jobs want the same single CPU. Their bursts are 2, 4 and 6 milliseconds and all arrive at time zero. Which order makes them wait least?

## The core concept

The scheduler allocates finite CPU time. We need a measurable objective, not just 'run jobs quickly'.

## Express it mathematically

$$
\bar W=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(S_i-A_i)
$$

**Every symbol explained:** W-bar is average waiting time in this simplified non-preemptive, single-burst setting; n is the number of jobs; S_i is job i's first start time; A_i is its arrival time; Σ means sum. If jobs block or are preempted, total ready-queue waiting requires additional accounting.

**Substitute actual numbers:** Order 2,4,6 gives starts 0,2,6. With arrivals 0,0,0 the waits are 0,2,6 and the average is (0+2+6)/3=8/3≈2.67 ms. Order 6,4,2 gives waits 0,6,10; average is 16/3≈5.33 ms.

## Why it works

Shortest-job-first minimises mean waiting time when all jobs arrive together and their burst sizes are known, under these assumptions. In a real system jobs arrive over time and lengths are unknown; short-first policies can starve long jobs.

## Go one level deeper

An interactive system also cares about response time and fairness. Linux scheduling policy details evolve; explain the objective before assuming a particular current algorithm.

## Common misunderstanding

A scheduler promising fairness is not the same as one minimising average wait. Try adding a continuous stream of tiny jobs and observe the starvation risk.

## Check your understanding

Explain the example with different numbers. Identify which assumption makes the derivation work, and which assumption would invalidate it. Then write the mathematical model again without looking.
